claim: Transformers trained only on bitstrings with random bit flips can still recover the exact noiseless rule for sparse majority functions over an odd number of bits and for sparse parities, which LSTMs largely cannot, because for these functions the best predictor of the label from noisy inputs is the target function itself. Supported only if, across 300 runs per noise rate with tuned random hyperparameters and 2,000-5,000 noisy training examples, the median transformer on Maj(20,5), Maj(40,5) and Maj(50,3) reaches close to the information-theoretic optimum on noisy validation data and beats the best of 300 LSTMs at moderate noise; if on Parity(20,4) transformers reach at least 95% noiseless accuracy more often than LSTMs at every non-zero noise rate even though both succeed comparably without noise; and if majority over an even number of bits, which is not its own optimal noisy predictor, loses noiseless accuracy faster.

experiments: Define noise-robust learning. Setup: uniform random bitstrings X, label Y = f(X), inputs corrupted by independent bit flips with probability p (labels never flipped); models are trained and validated on noisy pairs (Z, Y) and judged by accuracy on noiseless X. The Bayes-optimal noisy predictor is f* = sign(T_{1-2p} f), with T the noise operator; its error is bounded above and below by functions of H(Y|Z). Sensitivity sens[f] = sum over bits of the probability that flipping that bit changes f. Majority over an odd number of bits and parity are their own optimal noisy predictors (Proposition 1); for a uniformly random function, E[sens f*] ~ (n/pi) arccos(2p(1-p) / (p^2 + (1-p)^2)) < E[sens f] for p in (0, 1/2] (Proposition 2).

Fix models and training. Setup: encoder-only transformers (depth 1-6, width 16-128, 2-8 heads, dropout 0.05-0.1, absolute positions) and LSTMs (depth 1-6, hidden 16-128), Xavier init, cross-entropy, up to 1,000 epochs with early stopping after 300 epochs without validation improvement, model taken at best validation accuracy. Hyperparameter ranges are pruned on noiseless runs until at least about 70% of models learn the noiseless function, so failures under noise are not capacity failures; 300 runs with random initialisation and hyperparameters per noise rate; median parameter count about 32.5k (transformer) and 46.5k (LSTM) on parity.

Learn majorities and parity from noisy inputs. Setup: Maj(20,5), Maj(40,5), Maj(50,3) with 2,000 noisy training examples and 10,000 validation; Parity(20,4) with 5,000 training; noise rates in [0, 0.49). Result: without noise both architectures learn the majorities; at modest noise the median transformer sits close to the optimal noisy accuracy while the best of 300 LSTMs is worse; on Parity(20,4) outcomes are bimodal (learned or failed early), and transformers succeed more often than LSTMs at every non-zero noise rate, while LSTMs are practically never successful under noise (figures only).

Contrast with a function that is not self-predicting. Setup: Maj(30,4) (even number of relevant bits, so f* differs from f; at p = 0.32 f* is far more accurate on noisy data than f) under the same protocol. Result: transformers' noiseless accuracy degrades faster with noise than for odd-k majorities and LSTM accuracies become more bimodal; no model comes close to learning the true function.

Note the scope. Setup: noise is independent, identical bit flips on uniform inputs; the authors argue independent but non-identical noise should preserve sens[f*] <= sens[f], but correlated flips can raise the sensitivity of the smoothed function, so the conclusion need not hold for correlated noise; the effect needs noise rates high enough that f* != f, which may be rare in natural data; tasks are small synthetic Boolean functions with tiny models. Results are reported as distributions over random hyperparameters rather than a single tuned model, and the sensitivity-penalty success depends on a narrowly tuned lambda.
